event.title: South Asia pre-monsoon heat, India & Pakistan 2026
event.summary: From mid-April into May 2026, extreme pre-monsoon heat hit India and Pakistan. Many cities rose above 46°C. Outdoor workers and people in poor housing took the first harm. World Weather Attribution found human-caused climate change roughly tripled the chance of a comparable 15-day heatwave. It also made the heat about 0.9°C hotter.
event.hero: Hundreds of millions faced a longer, deadlier heat season.

nodes.title: Greenhouse gases are stretching the heat season earlier
nodes.description: Greenhouse gases trap extra heat over South Asia. World Weather Attribution finds April heat rising faster than May heat across the region. Dangerous temperatures now arrive earlier and last longer. That is a seasonal shift, not a single hot afternoon.

nodes.title: A 15-day extreme heat spell gripped the region
nodes.description: From mid-April into May 2026, many Indian cities saw daily maxima above 46°C. The analysed 15-day event was made about 3 times more likely by human-caused climate change. It was also about 0.9°C hotter. Northwestern India and Pakistan sat inside that spell together.

nodes.title: Humidity made the heat more dangerous
nodes.description: Irrigation and aerosols can offset some warming at the thermometer. They also raise humidity, so humid heat stress still climbs quickly. Bodies cool by sweating. Humid air takes that escape route away.

nodes.title: Heat killed and hospitalised the most exposed
nodes.description: Reporting cited by World Weather Attribution included at least 37 heat-related deaths in India. Ten more were reported in Karachi during the episode. Outdoor workers and people in poor housing face the highest risk. Those counts are preliminary, not a full excess-mortality estimate.

nodes.title: Electricity demand surged for cooling
nodes.description: India saw record-high electricity demand as cooling needs spiked during the heat. Grids built for a shorter heat season now face a longer one. Peak load is part of the ripple, not a separate story.

nodes.title: Agricultural drought compounded food risk
nodes.description: GDACS-linked reporting cited agricultural drought conditions affecting over 1 million km². That stress arrived before monsoon rains, when fields and wages are already tight. Heat and drought hit livelihoods in the same weeks.

nodes.title: Heat Action Plans help, but gaps remain
nodes.description: India and Pakistan have Heat Action Plans that prevent deaths when they are used. Heat is often not a notified disaster, which limits relief funding. Daily-wage workers remain exposed even where a plan exists on paper.

nodes.title: Lost work days hit the poorest first
nodes.description: When outdoor labour stops, household income drops immediately. That pathway is plausible even when national tallies lag. The people who cannot work indoors absorb the first economic hit.

nodes.title: Macroeconomic loss is not yet pinned to one figure here
nodes.description: Productivity and power-system costs are real pressures. A single GDP loss number is not treated as verified here. What is counted is the heat, the deaths reported, and the demand spike.

claims.text: A study measured how much more likely climate change made this. Combining observations and 19 validated climate models, World Weather Attribution found human-caused climate change roughly tripled the chance of a 15-day heatwave like April 2026. A comparable event was also about 0.9°C hotter than in a pre-industrial climate.
claims.geographic_scope: Northwestern India and Pakistan study region
claims.caveat: Uncertainty ranges are wide; synthesised factor ~3 (0.2 to 240).

claims.text: Aerosols and irrigation partially offset greenhouse warming at the thermometer. They also raise humidity. Dangerous humid heat continues to increase rapidly in the region.

Reporting cited by World Weather Attribution recorded at least 37 heat-related deaths in India. Ten heat-related deaths were reported in Karachi during the same episode. Outdoor workers and people in poor-quality housing are disproportionately exposed.
claims.caveat: Counts are preliminary media/agency figures, not a final excess-mortality study.

claims.text: The heat drove record-high electricity demand across India as cooling needs surged.
Agricultural drought conditions affecting over 1 million km² were reported by GDACS, as cited by World Weather Attribution. That stress compounded risks to food production and livelihoods.
claims.caveat: Drought extent is from GDACS-linked reporting cited by WWA.

claims.text: Heat Action Plans prevent deaths. They often lack context-specific guidelines. Because heatwaves are frequently not notified disasters, victims may be ineligible for disaster relief funding.
This is a reasonable link, but no study has confirmed a national income-loss total yet. Daily-wage and outdoor workers lose income when extreme heat stops work.
claims.geographic_scope: Urban and rural outdoor labour force

claims.text: Researchers are still studying the economic cost. No single verified macroeconomic loss figure for this 2026 South Asia heat episode is used here. Similar past events have disrupted livelihoods and local markets for months even when national GDP prints look small.
claims.methodology_status: trend estimate pending primary macro assessment

sources.title: Climate change exposes hundreds of millions to longer and deadlier pre-monsoon heat in South Asia

timeline.label: Heat intensifies
timeline.detail: From mid-April 2026, maxima above 46°C were recorded in many Indian cities. World Weather Attribution analysed a 15-day spell.

timeline.label: Power and health stress
timeline.detail: India saw record electricity demand. Heat-related deaths and hospital pressure were reported.

timeline.label: Attribution published
timeline.detail: World Weather Attribution found the event about 3 times more likely. It was also about 0.9°C hotter because of human-caused warming.

timeline.label: Farm and livelihood recovery
timeline.detail: Agricultural drought stress and lost work days continue into the monsoon transition.

timeline.label: Longer heat seasons ahead
timeline.detail: With further warming, similar events become still more likely and hotter. Heat Action Plans alone are not enough.

what_we_know: April-May 2026 brought extreme pre-monsoon heat across northwestern India and Pakistan.
Climate change roughly tripled the odds of a comparable 15-day event. It also added about 0.9°C.
Health impacts, power demand spikes, and agricultural drought stress were documented during the episode.
what_remains_uncertain: Final excess-mortality estimates beyond preliminary reported deaths.
Quantified household income losses for outdoor workers.
A single verified macroeconomic loss total for the episode.
